title: I can't code. I'm building a persistent multiplayer racing team manager with Claude Code, and here is what actually made it work
author: k2h1982
selftext:
I'm not a developer. I work in tech sales and I didn't touch any code for my school years, that's about it. Over the past few weeks I built Chicane Manager, a free browser game where you run a racing team in a persistent online championship: car design, drivers, money, and live strategy calls during a 3D race. It's about 20,000 lines of TypeScript (React, Three.js, a Node server), written entirely with Claude Code across roughly 200 commits. I never wrote a line myself.

I want to share what made the difference, because most of it had nothing to do with prompting.

**The first thing was treating it like a colleague with a bad memory**. I keep a short file of standing rules that gets loaded every session: never pause a live race, every visible text must exist in French and English, never deploy to production without my explicit go. Each rule came from a mistake that happened once. The file is the reason it didn't happen twice.

**The second was asking for scripts instead of trusting answers**. I can't review code, so I asked for tools that review the game for me. One script simulates full seasons and tells me if the economy drifts or if the AI teams become unbeatable. Another fails if any text is missing its translation. Before I see any UI change, it drives a real browser, takes a screenshot and looks at it. When it tells me "verified", I ask what exactly was verified and what wasn't. That one question caught more bugs than anything else.

**The third was two servers**. A sandbox where anything goes, and the real game, where real players have a season running. Every change lands on the sandbox first, I play it, then I say yes. It sounds obvious to developers. For a non-coder it was the single thing that let me ship daily without breaking a championship in progress.

**What didn't work: letting it design the game.** Left alone, it produces something reasonable and flat. Every decision that makes the game mine came from me playing and complaining. Two races a week because one felt too slow. A checklist for new players because my first testers were lost. A no-account trial because someone on Reddit told me a login wall was a hard sell, and he was right.

It's an alpha with a first full championship of 11 human players and a second one filling up. You can try it solo without an account at [https://chicanemanager.com](https://chicanemanager.com). To join the online championship, sign up with the invitation code **reddit-aigamedev**.

Happy to answer anything about the workflow, especially from other non-coders. What do you use to check work you can't read? Or do you even check work or just focus on the outputs and the "taste" of the game ?
